content: Chalicosis, also known as Flint disease, is a pulmonary condition primarily affecting the lungs or bronchioles. It occurs due to the inhalation of fine stone particles and is classified as a form of pneumoconiosis. The term chalicosis originates from the Greek word χάλιξ, meaning gravel, and was first introduced by Merkel in 1870 to describe pneumoconiosis caused by fine gravel or stone dust. This condition is most commonly observed in individuals working as stonecutters. The lungs are equipped with ciliated epithelium, mucus secretions, and phagocytes to protect the airways from dust particles. However, when exposed to excessive amounts of dust, the epithelium becomes overwhelmed and unable to filter all the particles. This leads to the leakage of dust into subpleural and interbronchial tissues, as well as the alveolar interspaces. The presence of these particles triggers an inflammatory response, resulting in the release of tumor necrosis factors, interleukin-1, leukotriene B4, and other cytokines. These mediators activate fibroblasts, which proliferate and produce collagen around the dust particles, ultimately causing fibrosis and the formation of nodular lesions in the lungs. Hepatosplenic involvement is not uncommon in cases of chalicosis. The primary cause of this condition is the inhalation of fine stone particles. It is essential to differentiate chalicosis from other diseases that cause pneumoconiosis or present with similar symptoms, such as cough, dyspnea, pulmonary nodules, and fibrosis on chest X-rays. Differential diagnoses include silicosis, asbestosis, tuberculosis, aspergillosis, and pulmonary malignancies. Occupational exposure to stone dust is a significant risk factor for chalicosis. High-risk occupations include those involving excavation in mines, mining of nonferrous metal ores, tunneling, quarrying, underground galleries, dry cutting, grinding, sieving, and handling of minerals and rocks. Other high-risk industries include foundry work, milling, sandblasting, and the pottery industry. Chalicosis is a slowly progressive disease, with clinical manifestations often taking up to 10 years to develop. Diagnosis requires a detailed occupational history, including the duration and intensity of exposure to stone dust, as well as measurements of respirable dust levels. Chest X-rays may reveal findings similar to those of pneumoconiosis, such as small rounded or irregular opacities, profusion of opacities, large opacities, zonal distribution of opacities (upper, middle, or lower zones), and pleural thickening (diffuse or circumscribed). Pulmonary function tests may show decreased total lung capacity (TLC), forced vital capacity (FVC), and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO), with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio. Symptoms of chalicosis include dyspnea, exertional dyspnea, and a chronic, non-productive cough. On physical examination, lung findings may include crackles (rales) and inspiratory wheezes. Other findings may include cyanosis and digital clubbing. Chest X-rays often reveal small rounded or irregular opacities, profusion of opacities, large opacities, and pleural thickening. These findings are similar to those seen in other conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or tuberculosis. There is no targeted therapy for chalicosis. Management focuses on avoiding further exposure to stone dust, optimizing respiratory function, and implementing preventive care. For acute symptom management, systemic steroids may be used. However, systemic steroids are not recommended for chronic management. Supplemental oxygen is administered to prevent complications of chronic hypoxemia, and bronchodilators may be prescribed if airflow limitation is detected on spirometry.
